messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Caleb Morrow is a 30-year-old carpenter and husband who presented for his first psychological evaluation approximately eight months after witnessing a serious industrial accident at a residential construction site where he had been working. He arrived visibly guarded, speaking in short sentences and frequently stopping mid-thought, as though the words themselves were obstacles he could not quite move around.

The event occurred on an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday morning. Caleb and a colleague, a man he had worked alongside for nearly three years, were framing the second floor of a new build when the scaffolding gave way. Caleb did not fall. His colleague did, landing on a partially assembled subfloor strewn with exposed nails and debris. Caleb was the first to reach him. He remembers pressing his hands against the man's torso to slow the bleeding — the warmth and wetness of it, the way the pressure of his own palms felt against torn skin — and he remembers the metallic taste in his mouth, which he later attributed to having bitten the inside of his cheek in the seconds after the fall. His colleague survived but required multiple surgeries and has not returned to work. Caleb has not spoken to him since.

In the weeks that followed, Caleb noticed that certain moments at work would stop him entirely. Passing a coworker with a gash from a utility knife, even a minor one, could bring the full scene back with a completeness that felt less like remembering and more like being returned there against his will. The memory did not arrive as a story he could tell himself; it arrived as sensation — the weight of his hands pressing down, the smell of sawdust and blood mixed together, the specific taste at the back of his throat. He has told his wife only that something happened at work and that he is dealing with it. When she has reached for him in ordinary moments of affection — a hand on his shoulder, her fingers brushing his arm — he has flinched or pulled away without meaning to, and he cannot explain to her why her touch feels, in those instants, like something he is not entitled to receive.

Over the following months, Caleb began eating heavily in the evenings, working through bags of chips or large second portions of dinner in a way he described as almost automatic, something his hands did while his mind went somewhere else. He has also developed a habit he finds shameful to describe: a deliberate effort, when distress becomes acute, to go somewhere inward and blank — to simply not be present in his own body. He does not have a name for what he is doing. He knows only that it offers a few minutes of relief and that he always comes back feeling worse.

He has almost entirely stopped thinking about the accident in any directed way, sidestepping the subject in his own mind with a consistency that has made it impossible to process what he witnessed. He told the intake clinician that he cannot seem to put what happened into a sentence that makes sense — that when he tries, the words feel wrong or too small, and he stops.

Caleb has come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he is not the same person he was before that morning. He was once someone who trusted his own hands, his own judgment, his own steadiness in a crisis. Now he is certain he cannot rely on himself in the ways that matter. He described his life as feeling broken in a way he does not expect to be fixed, and he used the word destroyed without drama, as a plain statement of fact. He fears the damage is permanent — not a wound that heals but a structural change, like a beam that has been stressed past its tolerance.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife telling him, gently but directly, that she felt she had lost him. He does not want to lose her. He arrived hoping, cautiously, that someone might help him find language for something that has so far existed only as sensation and dread.
